title: Hostility & Aggression
rule: Hostility words name an attitude (animosity, antipathy, enmity), a temperament (irascible), a bitter tone (acrimonious, rancorous), or open readiness to fight (belligerent, bellicose, pugnacious, truculent). The GRE usually tests them through contrast with courteous or conciliatory behavior (signals like 'though publicly cordial', 'far from', 'belied'), and it likes inimical in its sense of 'harmful or unfavorable to' something, not just 'unfriendly'.
tip: Bell- means war (Latin bellum) and pug- means fist (pugnus): a bellicose nation and a pugnacious person are both spoiling for a fight.

words.m: hostile and eager to fight or argue
words.s: Although the envoy had come to negotiate a truce, his belligerent tone at the opening session convinced his hosts that he was spoiling for a fight.

words.m: aggressively warlike; inclined to start fights or wars
words.s: The general's bellicose speeches, full of threats against neighboring states, alarmed diplomats who had hoped the new regime would pursue a quieter foreign policy.

words.m: eager or quick to quarrel, argue, or fight
words.s: A pugnacious critic who relished public feuds, she seemed to review books mainly to provoke their authors into angry rebuttals.

words.m: defiantly aggressive and eager to argue or fight
words.s: Questioned about the missing funds, the treasurer turned truculent, jabbing his finger at the auditors and daring them to prove anything.

words.m: angry and bitter, especially in speech or debate
words.s: What began as a polite scholarly disagreement became so acrimonious that the two historians refused to appear on the same conference panel.

words.m: marked by deep, long-lasting bitterness or resentment
words.s: Decades after the inheritance dispute, the siblings remained so rancorous that even a funeral could not bring them into the same room.
words.root: Latin rancor 'rankness, grudge'; feelings gone rancid

words.m: tending to obstruct or harm; unfriendly or hostile
words.s: Officials insisted the new surveillance rules protected the public, but civil libertarians argued that they were fundamentally inimical to a free press.

words.m: having or showing a wish to do evil to others
words.s: Readers long assumed the narrator's guardian was merely strict, but the final chapter reveals a truly malevolent figure who had plotted her ruin.

words.m: strong hostility or active dislike
words.s: The animosity between the two factions ran so deep that a minor procedural dispute nearly collapsed the coalition government.

words.m: a deep-seated feeling of aversion or dislike
words.s: Her antipathy toward bureaucracy was evident long before she took office; she had spent years mocking the very agencies she now ran.

words.m: easily made angry; hot-tempered
words.s: Though brilliant in the lab, the irascible professor would explode at students over trivial errors, so few dared to ask him questions.
words.root: Latin irasci 'to grow angry'; think ire

words.m: the state of being actively opposed or hostile to someone
words.s: The enmity between the rival dynasties outlasted every peace treaty, flaring into open war whenever one house sensed weakness in the other.

tc.q: Though the senator's public statements were unfailingly courteous, aides who worked with her privately described her as _____, prone to flare up at the slightest contradiction.
tc.why: 'Though... courteous' sets up a contrast, and 'prone to flare up at the slightest contradiction' defines irascible (quick-tempered). Placid and phlegmatic describe the calm the sentence denies; magnanimous and diffident do not involve anger.

tc.q: Far from being merely indifferent to scientific inquiry, the regime's policies were actively _____ to it, defunding laboratories and imprisoning researchers who published unwelcome findings.
tc.why: 'Far from merely indifferent... actively' calls for something stronger than indifference in the hostile direction, and defunding labs and jailing researchers shows harm: inimical. Conducive is the reversal trap; ancillary, germane, and tangential describe relevance, not hostility.

tc.q: The talks, which observers had expected to be (i) _____ given the two leaders' long history of public insults, proved surprisingly cordial; yet the communique's warm language may (ii) _____ an enmity that neither side has truly relinquished.
tc.why: A history of insults led observers to expect acrimonious talks, which 'proved surprisingly cordial' then reverses. Warm language cannot reveal (betray) or worsen (exacerbate) a hidden enmity; it can only mask it.

tc.q: Critics who dismissed the novelist's late essays as merely (i) _____ failed to notice that their combative surface concealed a deep (ii) _____ for the very institutions they attacked; she quarreled with the academy precisely because she loved it.
tc.why: 'Combative surface' tells you what critics saw: pugnacious essays. The final clause ('because she loved it') shows the concealed feeling was affection; antipathy is the trap because it matches the surface rather than what lies beneath it.

se.q: The ambassador's _____ remarks, which included a thinly veiled threat of military action, undid months of careful diplomacy.
se.why: A threat of military action makes the remarks bellicose or belligerent (warlike, hostile). Conciliatory and placatory are a synonym pair that contradicts the threat; enigmatic and verbose lack partners and miss the clue.

se.q: Although the two composers were publicly cordial, their private letters reveal a _____ that had festered for decades.
se.why: 'Although... publicly cordial' signals a hidden opposite, and 'festered' implies a growing ill will: animosity or enmity. Rapport and camaraderie are a matching pair, but they repeat the cordiality the sentence contrasts with.

se.q: The species is remarkably hardy, yet even it cannot survive in soils so acidic that they are _____ to nearly all plant life.
se.why: Soil that even a hardy species cannot survive in must be harmful to plants: inimical or hostile. Conducive and propitious form the trap pair, meaning the opposite; indifferent and amenable make no sense for soil chemistry.

se.q: Known for his _____ disposition, the coach was ejected from more games in a single season than most of his peers were in an entire career.
se.why: Record ejections imply a combative temperament: truculent or pugnacious. Equable and phlegmatic are a synonym pair meaning calm, the reverse of the clue; taciturn and magnanimous have no partner.

title: Calm & Composure
rule: These words describe inner steadiness under pressure (equanimity, imperturbable, unflappable, sangfroid, aplomb) or outward tranquility (placid, serene), and the GRE usually tests them by pitting a turbulent situation against a composed reaction ('even as the market plunged, she remained...'). Watch connotation: phlegmatic and stoic imply little visible emotion, dispassionate implies impartial reasoning, and nonchalant or insouciant suggest a casual lack of concern that can read as indifference.
tip: Sangfroid is French for 'cold blood' and equanimity is Latin for 'even mind' (aequus + animus): cool blood, level mind.

words.m: mental calmness and evenness of temper, especially under stress
words.s: She received news of the failed experiment with remarkable equanimity, calmly sketching a revised protocol while her colleagues lamented months of lost work.

words.m: unable to be upset or excited; extremely calm
words.s: Even as reporters shouted accusations at him, the imperturbable spokesman answered each question in the same level, unhurried voice.
words.root: Latin in- 'not' + perturbare 'to throw into confusion'

words.m: not easily upset or excited; calm and peaceful
words.s: The lake looked placid from the shore, but divers knew that strong currents churned just a few meters beneath its glassy surface.
words.root: Latin placere 'to please'; same root as placate

words.m: having an unemotional and stolidly calm disposition
words.s: Her phlegmatic temperament, which some mistook for indifference, made her ideal for emergency medicine, where panic helps no one.
words.root: Greek phlegma; the phlegm humor supposedly caused sluggish calm

words.m: enduring pain or hardship without showing feelings or complaining
words.s: The stoic farmer said little as the floodwaters destroyed his crops, simply beginning the next morning to clear debris from the fields.
words.root: Greek Stoa, the porch where Zeno taught endurance

words.m: self-confidence and assurance, especially in a demanding situation
words.s: When the projector failed midway through her keynote, she continued with such aplomb that many in the audience assumed the interruption had been planned.
words.root: French a plomb 'by the plumb line'; perfectly upright

words.m: composure or coolness under danger or trying circumstances
words.s: The pilot's sangfroid during the engine failure, calmly reciting procedures while passengers screamed, was later credited with saving everyone aboard.

words.m: having or showing calm in a crisis
words.s: Investors trusted the unflappable chief executive, who had steered the firm through three recessions without once appearing rattled in public.
words.root: un- + flap, slang for 'a state of agitation'

words.m: calm, peaceful, and untroubled
words.s: Amid the chaos of the evacuation, the elderly monk remained serene, walking slowly toward the boats as if nothing unusual were happening.

words.m: casually calm and relaxed; appearing unconcerned
words.s: His nonchalant reply to the committee's grave charges struck some as admirable composure, though others read it as contempt for the proceedings.

words.m: not influenced by strong emotion; rational and impartial
words.s: A good referee must offer a dispassionate assessment of the evidence, setting aside any sympathy for the author whose paper is under review.

words.m: showing a casual lack of concern; carefree
words.s: The heir's insouciant attitude toward money, tipping lavishly and never checking a bill, horrified the frugal accountants who managed his trust.

tc.q: The diplomat's _____ in the face of the protesters' jeers was all the more striking because, in private, she was known to agonize over even minor slights.
tc.why: 'All the more striking because, in private, she agonized' means her public reaction was the opposite of agonizing: poised composure, or aplomb. Trepidation and petulance would match her private anxiety and so would not be striking; rancor and vacillation miss the calm-versus-distress contrast.

tc.q: The physician's manner was so _____ that patients sometimes mistook her calm for coldness, though she was in fact deeply moved by their suffering.
tc.why: A manner calm enough to be mistaken for coldness is phlegmatic (unemotional, stolid). The other choices (effusive, frenetic, histrionic, mercurial) all suggest visible emotion or agitation, the opposite of the clue.

tc.q: Commentators praised the chess champion's (i) _____ during the final match, but her rival's camp contended that what looked like composure was in fact (ii) _____, an indifference to the outcome that bordered on disrespect for the game.
tc.why: The praised quality is the 'composure' later mentioned: sangfroid. The rival reframes it as 'an indifference to the outcome', which defines insouciance; trepidation (fear) and assiduity (diligence) do not match indifference.

tc.q: Ordinarily the most (i) _____ of observers, the veteran astronomer was so (ii) _____ by the anomalous readings that she telephoned her colleagues in the middle of the night.
tc.why: Phoning colleagues at midnight shows she was agitated, and 'ordinarily' signals that this was unlike her usual imperturbable self. Excitable would remove the contrast; unmoved and bored contradict the midnight calls.

se.q: Though the market plunged nearly twenty percent in a single afternoon, the veteran trader remained _____, quietly rebalancing her portfolio while younger colleagues panicked.
se.why: 'Quietly rebalancing' while others 'panicked' calls for calm: unflappable or imperturbable. Frantic and overwrought form a synonym pair describing the colleagues, not her; voluble and morose have no partner.

se.q: The memoirist recounts her years in the refugee camp with surprising _____, describing hunger and loss in the even tones one might use to report the weather.
se.why: 'Even tones' for terrible experiences signals calm: equanimity or composure. Bitterness and rancor are a matching pair but contradict the 'even tones'; levity means humor, which is not the same as evenness.

se.q: Critics who called the senator's response to the scandal _____ meant it as no compliment; to them, her apparent lack of concern signaled not composure but indifference to the victims.
se.why: 'Apparent lack of concern' that reads as indifference defines insouciant and nonchalant. Anguished and distraught are a synonym pair that means the opposite; contrite and scrupulous lack partners.

se.q: A historian must strive to be _____, weighing the evidence that offends her own sympathies as carefully as the evidence that flatters them.
se.why: Weighing evidence equally regardless of one's sympathies requires being dispassionate or objective. Partisan and tendentious are a synonym pair meaning the opposite; placid means calm but not impartial, so it has no true partner.

title: Caution vs. Rashness
rule: This cluster sets careful foresight (circumspect, prudent, chary, wary, judicious, vigilant) against hasty or careless boldness (impetuous, precipitate, foolhardy, rash, heedless, reckless). The GRE frames it with cause-and-effect clues (past losses make investors chary; acting before evidence is examined is precipitate) and with reversals such as 'no coward, but neither was he foolhardy'.
tip: Circum-spect means 'look around' before you act; pre-cipitate comes from 'headfirst' (prae + caput), so a precipitate decision dives in without looking.

words.m: wary and unwilling to take risks; carefully considering consequences
words.s: Having been burned by earlier scandals, the board became circumspect, refusing to approve any acquisition until outside auditors had examined every account.

words.m: acting with care and thought for the future
words.s: With interest rates likely to rise, the prudent course was to pay down the debt rather than borrow even more for expansion.

words.m: cautiously reluctant or wary about doing something
words.s: Scientists are understandably chary of announcing a cure after only a single small trial, since early results so often fail to replicate.
words.root: Old English cearig 'careful'; related to care

words.m: feeling or showing caution about possible dangers or problems
words.s: Voters had grown wary of sweeping promises, having watched the previous administration abandon nearly every pledge within its first year.
words.root: Old English waer 'aware'; same root as beware

words.m: having, showing, or done with good judgment
words.s: Through judicious editing, she reduced the unwieldy manuscript by a third without sacrificing a single essential argument.

words.m: keeping careful watch for possible danger or difficulty
words.s: Public health officials remained vigilant long after the outbreak subsided, testing water supplies weekly for any sign of renewed contamination.

words.m: acting quickly and without thought or care
words.s: Her impetuous decision to quit the firm the very afternoon she was passed over for promotion left her without income for nearly a year.

words.m: recklessly bold; taking foolish risks
words.s: Mountaineers considered it foolhardy to attempt the summit so late in the season, when sudden storms could trap climbers for days.

words.m: done or acting suddenly, without careful consideration
words.s: Critics warned that a precipitate withdrawal of troops, undertaken before local forces were trained, could plunge the region into chaos.

words.m: acting or done without careful consideration of the consequences
words.s: It would be rash to conclude from a single survey that public opinion has shifted, since the sample was small and the questions poorly worded.

words.m: showing a careless lack of attention or regard
words.s: Heedless of the warnings posted along the trail, the hikers wandered onto the crumbling ledge to photograph the waterfall below.

words.m: without thinking or caring about the consequences of an action
words.s: The bank's reckless lending, which extended mortgages to borrowers with no verified income, eventually forced a costly government rescue.

tc.q: Given how often early findings in the field have failed to replicate, the researchers were _____ about publicizing their preliminary results, insisting on a second, larger trial first.
tc.why: Insisting on a second trial before going public shows cautious reluctance: chary. Sanguine, voluble, and ebullient imply eagerness to share; cavalier implies the careless attitude the researchers avoid.

tc.q: The committee's decision, made within hours of the allegation and before any evidence had been examined, was widely criticized as _____.
tc.why: Deciding 'within hours' and 'before any evidence had been examined' is the definition of precipitate (overhasty). Judicious, circumspect, and meticulous describe the care that was missing; belated is the opposite of hasty.

tc.q: Although she was often accused of being (i) _____, the entrepreneur's apparently impulsive ventures were in fact preceded by months of (ii) _____ research that her critics never saw.
tc.why: The accusation matches the 'apparently impulsive' ventures: reckless. 'Although... in fact' reverses it, so the hidden research must have been careful: painstaking. Cursory and desultory would confirm the critics rather than refute them.

tc.q: The general was no coward, but neither was he (i) _____: he would commit troops only after scouts had confirmed the enemy's position, a (ii) _____ that frustrated his more impetuous subordinates but saved countless lives.
tc.why: 'No coward, but neither...' requires the opposite extreme of cowardice: foolhardy (pusillanimous means cowardly). Waiting for confirmed intelligence is prudence; temerity is rashness, and lethargy misreads deliberate caution as sluggishness and would not 'save lives'.

se.q: Investors who had lost fortunes in the previous crash were understandably _____ when presented with any scheme promising extraordinary returns.
se.why: Past losses ('understandably') make investors cautious: wary or chary. Credulous and gullible form a synonym pair, but they reverse the logic; ebullient and nostalgic have no partner.

se.q: The memo warned that any _____ response to the cyberattack, launched before investigators had identified its source, might provoke retaliation against the wrong target.
se.why: A response 'launched before investigators had identified its source' is hasty: precipitate or impetuous. Measured and deliberate are a synonym pair describing the opposite; belated and proportionate do not capture haste.

se.q: A _____ editor, she cut only what was genuinely superfluous, preserving the author's voice while sharpening every argument.
se.why: Cutting 'only what was genuinely superfluous' shows good judgment: judicious or discerning. Slapdash and careless are a synonym pair that contradicts the clue; heavy-handed has no partner and also contradicts it.

se.q: The yacht's crew, _____ of the forecasters' warnings, set out into the gathering storm and had to be rescued by the coast guard two days later.
se.why: Sailing into a storm despite warnings shows the crew paid no attention: heedless or oblivious. Mindful and wary (and chary) suggest caution, which their actions contradict; enamored makes no sense.

title: Diligence vs. Idleness
rule: This cluster contrasts sustained, careful effort (assiduous, sedulous, diligent, industrious, indefatigable, painstaking) with laziness or low energy (indolent, lethargic, torpor) and half-hearted work (lackadaisical, desultory, perfunctory). GRE items often depend on how the work was done: perfunctory means done with minimal care and desultory means aimless or unsystematic, so neither means 'not done at all'.
tip: Assiduous comes from 'sitting at' (ad + sedere) your desk; in-dolent means 'not feeling pain', because the indolent never exert themselves enough to hurt.

words.m: showing great care and persistent effort
words.s: Years of assiduous research in provincial archives allowed the historian to reconstruct the daily lives of peasants whom earlier scholars had ignored.
words.root: Latin assidere 'to sit beside'; sits at the task

words.m: showing dedication and steady diligence
words.s: The sedulous apprentice copied each of his master's sketches dozens of times, refusing to move on until every line was perfect.
words.root: Latin sedulus 'zealous', from se dolo 'without guile'

words.m: having or showing care and conscientiousness in one's work
words.s: A diligent reviewer, he checked every citation in the manuscript and discovered that several key quotations had been taken out of context.

words.m: hardworking and steadily busy
words.s: The industrious villagers terraced the steep hillsides by hand, transforming barren slopes into fields that fed the region for centuries.

words.m: persisting tirelessly; incapable of being worn out
words.s: The indefatigable activist spoke at dozens of rallies each month, often traveling through the night to reach the next town by morning.

words.m: done with or employing great care and thoroughness
words.s: The painstaking restoration of the fresco took eleven years, as conservators removed centuries of grime one square centimeter at a time.

words.m: wanting to avoid activity or exertion; lazy
words.s: The novel's indolent aristocrat spends his mornings in bed and his afternoons in cafes, roused to action only when his allowance runs short.

words.m: sluggish and apathetic; lacking energy
words.s: After weeks of sleepless nights, the normally energetic reporter became lethargic, missing deadlines and barely responding to her editor's messages.

words.m: a state of physical or mental inactivity; sluggishness
words.s: The long summer afternoons induced a kind of torpor in the town, and even the shopkeepers dozed behind their counters.

words.m: lacking enthusiasm and determination; carelessly lazy
words.s: The coach blamed the defeat on the team's lackadaisical practice sessions, during which players often wandered off before drills were finished.
words.root: from lackaday, an old sigh of weary regret

words.m: lacking a plan, purpose, or enthusiasm; jumping randomly between things
words.s: His desultory reading, a chapter of history here and a few poems there, left him with scattered facts but no coherent understanding of any subject.
words.root: Latin desultor, a circus rider leaping between horses

words.m: carried out with minimum effort or reflection
words.s: The inspector gave the factory only a perfunctory glance before signing the certificate, never opening the doors behind which the violations lay.
words.root: Latin perfungi 'to get through with, discharge'

tc.q: Though her biography of the poet was hailed for its _____ scholarship, some reviewers felt that the sheer accumulation of meticulously verified detail obscured any larger interpretation.
tc.why: The praised quality is the 'meticulously verified detail' that reviewers later fault: painstaking scholarship. Desultory, slipshod, and cursory are the opposite of meticulous, and tendentious (biased) is not supported by the clue.

tc.q: The governor's investigation into the bridge collapse was so _____ that it ended after a single afternoon of interviews, prompting calls for an independent inquiry.
tc.why: 'So _____ that it ended after a single afternoon' requires minimal effort: perfunctory. Exhaustive and assiduous reverse the clue; partisan and belated do not explain the brevity.

tc.q: Visitors who saw only the scientist's (i) _____ demeanor, his slow speech and seemingly drowsy gaze, were astonished to learn that he was among the most (ii) _____ researchers in the institute, routinely working eighteen-hour days.
tc.why: 'Slow speech and seemingly drowsy gaze' describe a lethargic demeanor. 'Astonished' and 'eighteen-hour days' demand the opposite: indefatigable. Indolent and dilatory would not astonish anyone, since they match the demeanor.

tc.q: Far from being the (i) _____ dilettante his detractors portrayed, the collector pursued his interests with (ii) _____ dedication, cataloging each acquisition in exhaustive notebooks over five decades.
tc.why: The detractors' portrait of a dilettante calls for a dismissive adjective: desultory (aimless, dabbling). 'Far from' plus five decades of exhaustive notebooks demands sedulous dedication; fitful and perfunctory would confirm the detractors.

se.q: Though gifted, the young pianist was too _____ to master the concerto, practicing only when she felt like it and abandoning difficult passages after a few attempts.
se.why: Practicing only on a whim and quickly giving up shows laziness or lack of determination: indolent or lackadaisical. Assiduous and sedulous form a synonym pair that contradicts the clue; precocious matches 'gifted' but does not explain her failure.

se.q: Thanks to the _____ efforts of volunteers who combed the shoreline every morning for months, the endangered turtles' nesting sites were finally mapped.
se.why: Combing the shore 'every morning for months' is unflagging effort: tireless or indefatigable. Desultory, perfunctory, and sporadic contradict the steady routine; lavish does not describe persistence.

se.q: The audit was _____ at best: the examiners glanced at summary figures, skipped the supporting documents entirely, and signed off within an hour.
se.why: Glancing, skipping documents, and finishing within an hour describe minimal effort: cursory or perfunctory. Scrupulous and thorough are a synonym pair meaning the opposite; erroneous may be a result, but it does not describe the effort and has no partner.

se.q: The heat had induced a general _____ in the camp; soldiers who ordinarily drilled at dawn now lay in the shade until evening.
se.why: Lying in the shade instead of drilling shows sluggish inactivity: torpor or lethargy. Fervor and zeal form a synonym pair that reverses the clue; anxiety and discord are unsupported.

title: Skill vs. Ineptitude
rule: Skill words range from physical nimbleness (deft, dexterous) to mental or social agility (adroit, adept, proficient) to complete mastery (consummate, virtuoso), while their opposites name clumsiness (maladroit, inept, gauche, bungle) or mere dabbling (dilettante). GRE items often hinge on the gap between apparent and real competence (a supposed dilettante revealed as a master) and on paired forms such as adroit/maladroit and adept/inept.
tip: Right is skillful and left is awkward: dexter and adroit both point 'to the right', while gauche is French for 'left'.

words.m: clever or skillful in using the hands or mind
words.s: An adroit negotiator, she persuaded both unions to accept the contract by framing each concession as a victory for their own members.
words.root: French a droit 'to the right', i.e., right-handed

words.m: neatly skillful and quick in movement or handling
words.s: With a few deft strokes of the brush, the calligrapher produced a character that her students had struggled for weeks to imitate.
words.root: Middle English variant of daft, once meaning 'apt'

words.m: showing or having skill, especially with the hands
words.s: The surgeon's dexterous handling of the tiny vessels allowed her to complete in two hours an operation that typically takes five.

words.m: very skilled or proficient at something
words.s: Adept at reading a hostile audience, the lecturer abandoned her prepared remarks and won over the skeptics with a series of pointed questions.

words.m: competent or skilled in doing or using something
words.s: Although she was proficient in four languages, the translator insisted that true fluency required years of living among native speakers.

words.m: a person highly skilled in music or another art
words.s: A virtuoso of the violin by the age of twelve, he later confessed that his technical brilliance had long masked a shallow musical understanding.
words.root: Italian virtuoso 'skilled, learned', from Latin virtus

words.m: showing great skill and flair; complete or perfect
words.s: Even critics who disliked the play conceded that the lead actor was a consummate professional, never missing a cue in two hundred performances.
words.root: Latin consummare 'to bring to the sum, complete'

words.m: ineffective or bungling; clumsy
words.s: The minister's maladroit handling of the crisis, which included blaming victims on live television, cost the government its majority.

words.m: having or showing no skill; clumsy or incompetent
words.s: The inept repair crew managed to flood the basement while attempting to fix a minor leak in the kitchen sink.

words.m: lacking ease or grace; socially awkward and tactless
words.s: Raised far from society, the young heir made a series of gauche remarks at his first formal dinner, including asking the hostess the price of her necklace.

words.m: to carry out a task clumsily or incompetently
words.s: Investigators feared that inexperienced officers would bungle the collection of evidence, rendering it inadmissible in court.

words.m: a dabbler in an art or field who lacks serious knowledge
words.s: Professional historians dismissed him as a dilettante, noting that his sweeping theories rested on a handful of secondary sources read in translation.
words.root: Italian dilettare 'to delight'; dabbles for pleasure

tc.q: Though reviewers praised the debut novelist's _____ handling of multiple narrators, they found the plot itself clumsy and predictable.
tc.why: 'Though... praised' contrasts with 'clumsy', so the praised handling must be skillful: deft. Maladroit and gauche mean clumsy, matching the criticism instead of contrasting with it; hackneyed and timorous are not praise.

tc.q: The ambassador was recalled not because he was malicious but because he was hopelessly _____: in a single week he insulted the host country's prime minister, misplaced classified cables, and missed a summit he had himself arranged.
tc.why: The list of blunders (gaffes, lost cables, a missed summit) shows incompetence, not ill will: inept. Duplicitous and avaricious imply the kind of bad intent the sentence rules out; intransigent and timid do not explain misplacing cables or missing meetings.

tc.q: The critic's charge that the composer was a mere (i) _____ seems difficult to sustain; his sketchbooks show decades of rigorous study, and his late quartets display a (ii) _____ command of counterpoint that few professionals could match.
tc.why: 'A mere ___' plus evidence of decades of rigorous study that refutes the charge points to dilettante (dabbler). A command 'few professionals could match' is consummate; rudimentary and tenuous would support the critic.

tc.q: Socially (i) _____ but technically brilliant, the engineer was at her best in the laboratory, where her (ii) _____ fingers could assemble circuits too delicate for anyone else to handle.
tc.why: 'But technically brilliant' and 'at her best in the laboratory' imply social weakness: gauche. Assembling circuits too delicate for others requires dexterous fingers; urbane and adroit remove the contrast, and maladroit contradicts it.

se.q: Even her rivals admitted that the senator was _____ at parliamentary tactics, able to turn an opponent's procedural maneuver into an opportunity for her own legislation.
se.why: Turning an opponent's maneuver to her own advantage shows skill: adept or adroit. Inept and clumsy are a synonym pair that contradicts 'even her rivals admitted'; reticent and censorious have no partner.

se.q: Officials feared that the hastily assembled crew would _____ the rescue, and their worst fears were realized when it drilled into a flooded shaft it had failed to locate on its own maps.
se.why: A blunder that confirms 'worst fears' about a hasty crew means the rescue was mishandled: bungle or botch. Expedite and facilitate are a synonym pair with the wrong charge; abandon does not match drilling into a shaft.

se.q: His _____ attempt to apologize, which consisted mainly of explaining why the offended guests had misunderstood him, only deepened the rift.
se.why: An apology that blames the listeners and deepens the rift is clumsy and tactless: maladroit or gauche. Graceful and tactful form the opposite synonym pair; sincere and terse lack partners and do not explain the failure.

se.q: A true _____ of the keyboard, she could play the most demanding etudes at sight, yet she was equally admired for the restraint of her interpretations.
se.why: Sight-reading the hardest etudes marks a master: virtuoso or maestro. Dilettante and dabbler are a synonym pair that contradicts 'a true ___'; novice and critic do not fit.

title: Support vs. Undermine
rule: These verbs describe what evidence or argument does to a claim: strengthen it (corroborate, substantiate, bolster, buttress, underpin, vindicate) or weaken it (undermine, vitiate, rebut, refute, debunk, gainsay). On the GRE, track the direction of the logic carefully ('far from vindicating the theory, the letters undermined it'), and remember that refute means to prove false, which is stronger than rebut, to argue against.
tip: Think architecture: buttress, underpin, and bolster prop a claim up, while under-mine digs a tunnel beneath its walls.

words.m: to confirm or give support to a statement or finding
words.s: Two independent laboratories were able to corroborate the original findings, finally silencing those who had attributed the results to contamination.

words.m: to provide evidence that supports or proves the truth of
words.s: The reporter refused to publish the allegation until she could substantiate it with documents rather than rely on a single anonymous source.
words.root: Latin substantia 'substance'; give a claim substance

words.m: to support or strengthen; to prop up
words.s: The senator cited the new unemployment figures to bolster her argument that the stimulus package had been too small to matter.

words.m: to increase the strength of or justification for; reinforce
words.s: The author attempts to buttress her controversial thesis with an appendix of statistics, but most of the figures are decades out of date.
words.root: Old French bouterez 'thrusting'; a stone wall support

words.m: to show to be right or justified; to clear of blame
words.s: Later excavations would vindicate the archaeologist, whose once-ridiculed claim of a Bronze Age settlement beneath the city proved entirely correct.

words.m: to support, justify, or form the basis for
words.s: The assumption that consumers always act rationally, which once seemed to underpin all of economics, has been challenged by decades of behavioral research.
words.root: under + pin; to prop up a wall from below

words.m: to weaken or damage, especially gradually or insidiously
words.s: Revelations that the lead investigator had falsified data did more to undermine public trust in the study than any critic's argument could have.
words.root: to dig a mine beneath a fortress wall

words.m: to prove a statement or theory to be wrong
words.s: Rather than merely deny the accusation, the defense set out to refute it, producing receipts proving the defendant was abroad that week.

words.m: to argue against or offer evidence contradicting an accusation
words.s: Given only five minutes, the junior scholar could not fully rebut the panel's objections, though she promised a detailed response in writing.

words.m: to expose the falseness or hollowness of an idea or belief
words.s: The magician devoted his retirement to an effort to debunk the spiritualists, reproducing their supposed miracles with ordinary stage tricks.

words.m: to deny or contradict; to speak against
words.s: No one could gainsay the scale of her achievement, though critics continued to question whether her methods were entirely ethical.

words.m: to spoil or impair the quality of; to invalidate
words.s: A single unexamined assumption can vitiate an otherwise rigorous proof, rendering every subsequent step logically worthless.

tc.q: Although the defendant's story seemed implausible at first, the security footage would ultimately _____ every detail of his account, down to the color of the jacket he claimed to have worn.
tc.why: 'Although... implausible at first' sets up a reversal: the footage confirmed his story, down to the smallest detail, so corroborate. Undermine and impugn continue the initial doubt instead of reversing it; embellish and obfuscate make no sense for footage.

tc.q: The discovery that the sample had been drawn almost entirely from a single, unrepresentative hospital threatens to _____ the study's conclusions, once widely cited.
tc.why: An unrepresentative sample is a methodological flaw that 'threatens' the conclusions, so it would vitiate (impair, invalidate) them. Buttress and vindicate reverse the direction; anticipate and popularize ignore the flaw.

tc.q: Proponents hailed the newly unearthed letters as evidence that would (i) _____ the long-disputed theory of the poet's authorship; on closer inspection, however, the letters' anachronistic vocabulary served only to (ii) _____ it.
tc.why: Proponents of a disputed theory would hail evidence that vindicates it. 'However' and anachronistic vocabulary (a sign of forgery) reverse that, so the letters undermine the theory; substantiate is the trap that ignores the 'however'.

tc.q: Few would (i) _____ that the reforms reduced crime in their first year; what remains in dispute is whether that single year of data, which the mayor cites incessantly, can (ii) _____ his far bolder claim that the gains will persist after federal funding expires.
tc.why: 'What remains in dispute' implies the first-year drop is not disputed, so few would gainsay (deny) it; concede would mean the opposite. The mayor cites the data in support of his claim, so the open question is whether they can bolster it; rebut reverses his purpose.

se.q: The pilot program's results did little to _____ the reformers' optimism; if anything, they suggested that the proposed curriculum might actually lower test scores.
se.why: 'If anything' pushes further in the direction opposite the blank: results that suggest lower scores did little to support the optimism, so bolster or buttress. Temper and dampen form a synonym pair that would make 'if anything' illogical, since such results would dampen optimism.

se.q: Critics hoped the newly declassified files would _____ the official account of the incident, but the documents instead confirmed nearly every detail of it.
se.why: 'But... instead confirmed' means the critics hoped for the opposite of confirmation: debunk or refute. Corroborate and substantiate are a synonym pair describing what actually happened, not what critics hoped.

se.q: A single procedural error was enough to _____ the prosecution's case: because the warrant had been improperly signed, all evidence gathered under it was excluded.
se.why: Losing all evidence from an invalid warrant damages the case: vitiate or undermine. Bolster and corroborate are a synonym pair with the wrong direction; prolong and publicize have no partner and miss the clue.

se.q: Decades after his conviction, DNA evidence would _____ the prisoner, whose claims of innocence had long been dismissed as the desperate fictions of a guilty man.
se.why: The structure implies the long-dismissed claims of innocence were proven true: vindicate or exonerate. Incriminate and implicate are a synonym pair that would confirm the dismissal, not overturn it.
